name: MBC Arheilgen
body:
Closest flying ground to the city, and multicopters are named in the club's own permitted-types list. Guest flying is €5 a day with prior permission.

Two catches: the field is only 120 × 80 m, and the flight rules still carry 2010-era wording demanding the model stay continuously visible — so expect a conversation about goggles and a spotter.
next: Ring ahead for a guest slot — but read Trebur first if you want goggles without negotiation.

name: Modellflieger Griesheim
body:
The closest club that spells out “Quad-/Multikopter” in its own membership text. Clearly alive — club night every Wednesday at 20:00 — and around €125 a year.

Correction worth knowing: their indoor sessions in the Hegelsberghalle are members only, with non-flying spectators admitted by prior email. But they built two gates out of pool noodles as a precision course explicitly “for quadcopters as well as planes” — so this is the local club that already thinks about multirotors.

FPV itself isn't mentioned either way, so goggles are an ask rather than a given.
next: Join rather than visit — then the pool-noodle gate course is yours on Wednesdays.

name: MFC Weiterstadt
body: A registered DMFV site very close to town, so multirotors are permitted in principle. The club's own website says nothing about copters or FPV and carries no recent dates.
next: Lowest-information option nearby — worth a call, but not before Griesheim or Dieburg.

name: FMV Dieburg 1970
body:
The warmest public language about multirotors anywhere in the region — gliders, powered fixed-wing, “Multikoptern (Drohnen)” and helicopters, all flyable. Guest flying is free with proof of insurance.

Event activity through 2025 and a registry edit in March 2026 confirm it's running.
next: The easiest first phone call on the whole map.

name: SFC Darmstadt — Ober-Ramstadt
body:
Darmstadt's own model flying club, with a registered field at Ober-Ramstadt plus sites at Messel, and over 150 model members. Demonstrably active — a flying day advertised for 2026 and a club photo posted in late July.

Their material never mentions multicopters, drones or FPV, so the policy is genuinely unknown rather than permissive.
next: Email and ask directly whether goggles are allowed — they're the nearest large club.

name: SFC Messel + indoor hall
body:
An outdoor field plus an indoor venue — the nearest indoor session to you at around 10 km, running every second Sunday in season.

The decisive detail: for 2025/26 the club bought Droneball Sweeper units to run F9A Drone Ball. They are actively bringing multirotors into their hall, which makes this the most promising unasked question on the map.

Hall address isn't published and the guest policy is unverified.
next: Ring or email the club about the Drone Ball sessions — best close-in lead I have.

name: MFC Langen
body: Registered DMFV site, so multirotors are permitted in principle. Clearly active with an AGM in March 2026 and an event in May. Nothing published about FPV.
next: Fallback option north of the city.

name: MFSV Trebur
body:
The only site in the region that permits FPV in writing. Its field rules set it out explicitly: goggles up to 30 m within normal visual range, up to 120 m with an additional airspace observer, nothing above 120 m.

Permit issued by Regierungspräsidium Darmstadt, with a DFS arrangement allowing 150 m and up to 300 m by phone clearance from the Frankfurt tower. Very active — hosting a heli championship in September 2026, and a university used the site for drone testing in late 2025.

Downside: open grass. Nothing to fly around.
next: Join here if you want the goggles question settled before you arrive.

name: Saalflugverein Rodgau — indoor
body:
For actual proximity freestyle this is the most realistic answer on the map. The club explicitly flies “Multikoptern (Drohnen)” and notes that drones are flown by several pilots simultaneously.

Thursdays 19:00–22:00, October to March, at the Bürgerhaus on Römerstraße. Guests and visiting pilots are explicitly welcome — bring insurance proof on your first visit.

A hall has beams, doorways and walls — German outdoor model fields are mown strips with nothing to fly around, which is why this beats sites twice as close.
next: Email the hall address before the season opens in October.

name: MFG Bensheim
body:
Read this one carefully. Outdoor FPV is forbidden by the site's own permit, not by club preference — so it cannot be waved through locally.

Their indoor hall is a different matter: the hall rules govern helis and multicopters alongside fixed-wing, and a 2026 revision was published in March.
next: Indoor yes, outdoor no. Don't waste a trip on the field.

name: TuS Massenheim — FPV section
body:
The only formally organised FPV section in Rhein-Main — a real department of a sports club, founded in 2022, confirmed still running via a January 2026 exchange.

Indoor, whoops up to 3.5" and sub-250 g, with larger 5" planned. Beginners explicitly welcome and trial sessions available on request. Tuesdays at 20:00.

No competitions — this is a flying group, not a race scene.
next: Ask for a trial session via the club's FPV page.

name: Weilbachhalle — indoor
body:
Year-round indoor flying with quadcopters explicitly permitted — up to eight at once — Wednesdays 09:00–12:00, plus Sunday mornings that move outdoors from May to September.

Guests welcome for up to three visits at €5 each, and the schedule is published through 30 December 2026. Not FPV-specific.
next: Three guest visits means you can try it without joining anything.

name: FPV-Racer Bodenheim
body: An established indoor FPV racing group going since 2015. A January 2026 post puts them in the large gymnasium of the Nackenheim Gymnasium, Fridays from 18:30, flying racers, whoops, longrange and custom builds.
next: Message their page, or reply in the Mainz/Worms forum thread.

name: FMCM Drohnen Race Cup
body:
The closest real FPV event of the year, and it's twelve days out: Sunday 16 August 2026, 13:00, at the club's “An der kleinen Loh” field.

Open to 3–5" quads on analog, HDZero, Walksnail or DJI O4 race mode. Grill on site — bring your own meat. The club also states guests may fly if insured.

The announcement went up on 4 August 2026, so this club is unambiguously live.
next: Email headcount to the club by 14 August. This is the single best move this month.

name: LSV Lindenfels — indoor
body:
Indoor season starts 7 November 2026 with an opening session, then weekly on Saturdays at 17:15, plus an indoor flying competition in January.

One of only a handful of clubs in the region that has already published next season's dates. Multirotor policy not stated — ask.
next: Diarise 7 November and email before then.

name: MFC Nierstein-Oppenheim — indoor
body:
Almost every Sunday from 14:30 to 17:00, November to March, in the Oppenheim grammar-school sports hall.

A reliable weekly slot west of the Rhine. Multirotor policy needs confirming.
next: Ask whether copters are welcome before the season starts.

name: Kelkheimer Luftsport-Club — indoor
body: Every Sunday 17:00–19:30 through the winter in the Pestalozzischule sports hall. The club's registered permitted types include multicopters and helicopters.
next: Published phone and secretary email — straightforward enquiry.

name: MBC Hanau-Ronneburg — indoor
body:
States its indoor sessions cover shock-flyers, small helicopters and quadcopters, and says plainly that every guest is welcome.

Further out, but one of the few halls that names copters and invites visitors in the same breath.
next: Turn up as a guest — they've said yes in advance.

name: MSC Schöneck — indoor
body:
Generous hours — Saturdays 09:00–10:00 and 11:00–14:00, Sundays 18:00–22:00 — but note the hard 300 g all-up weight limit, which applies to all disciplines.

That means 65–75 mm whoops and small 2–3" builds. No 5" freestyle quad will be allowed in. Parts of their page are stale, so confirm dates.
next: Only worth the trip if you own or fancy a whoop.

name: Steinbruch am Roßberg
body:
Quarried from 1898 to 2010 and now inactive: 500 m across, 120 m deep, four extraction levels and a roughly 100 m wall of basalt columns. A huge vertical void eight kilometres from your door.

Not architecture — no halls or stairwells — but quarries are exactly the site type German FPV pilots actually fly.

Owned by OHI/MHI, headquartered in Darmstadt; their only working pits are elsewhere.
next: An annual guided geological excursion runs at €5 with registration, and its organiser already holds the owner relationship. That's your introduction.

name: Eisenbahnmuseum Kranichstein
body:
I'd written this off as a working museum, then found it sells bookable photo access outside normal tour hours.

What you'd be flying: a 1908/1912 sixteen-stall roundhouse with turntable, coal bunkers and brick halls, the whole site listed as a protected ensemble. A radial engine shed is close to ideal proximity geometry.

Note the adjacent former marshalling yard is now an active DB construction site for a long-distance train depot.
next: The only way to fly a roundhouse in this region legally. Ask about out-of-hours photo access.

name: Spitzbunker on the Knell
body:
Four conical WWII air-raid towers survive in the city, monument-protected, with 1.9 m reinforced concrete walls. The municipal services own the Knell site and one tower can be entered by arrangement; the other is sealed.

Honest assessment: a conical interior is poor freestyle geometry. But it is a legal, bookable vertical shaft ten minutes away — sources disagree on whether it's eleven storeys or fifteen.
next: Contact the municipal services (EAD) about the enterable tower.

name: ESOC ground station
body:
A 15 m parabolic antenna and one building. Small, but there is nothing else like it in the region.

The owner is running a conversion project explicitly aimed at legal public access, with a named architect leading it — the best odds of a friendly yes anywhere on this map.

Under video surveillance, and surrounded by a 50 ha private biotope, so the nature side needs care.
next: Approach the conversion project directly rather than the site.

name: Opel-Altwerk
body:
A genuinely large historic industrial complex, documented from inside by local press as a lost place, with Motorworld now redeveloping it into an “Erlebniswelt”.

The reason it's here: this owner says yes. An art biennale in May 2026, a KunstSalon, a MakerSpace, graffiti and painting projects, a 700-oldtimer meet, a classic-car event in the old forge. That is a landlord you can actually ask.

The catch is airspace — unlike Darmstadt, Rüsselsheim falls inside the Frankfurt control zone, where a new four-zone DFS procedure took effect on 6 August 2026.
next: Permission plus a control-zone clearance. A project, not a spontaneous session.

name: Opel-Rennbahn
body:
Germany's first purpose-built concrete speed bowl, opened 1919 — and the banked curves are still there in the forest. Part of the track has been cleared and given a viewing platform right at the Steilkurve, so the structure reads rather than being buried in scrub.

Freely accessible woodland, open around the clock, 4.4 from 416 reviews — ten of which call it a lost place. As terrain it is a proximity spot, not a bando: banked concrete, trees, gaps, no interior.

⚠️ The catch is airspace, not access. It sits inside the Frankfurt control zone, same as the Opel-Altwerk 2.5 km north. Nothing stops you walking in; flying needs a clearance.
next: The ground needs no permission from anyone. Get the control-zone clearance first — that is the entire problem here.

name: Hochofen Gräfenbacherhütte
body:
A 19th-century blast furnace standing in woodland — masonry stack and works remains, an industrial monument rather than another castle ruin, which is what makes it worth the drive west. Open around the clock, unfenced, 4.4 from 32 reviews, with a supporters' group at hochofenfreunde.de.

Reviewers note it is decaying steadily and that winter or early spring is the time to come, because the trees close the sightlines for the rest of the year — which happens to be the flying advice too.
next: No owner gate found, no fence, no fee. Check the Soonwald nature-protection status before you drive — that is the one thing I could not settle from the desk.

name: Klinik Lohrey
body:
A 180-bed private rehab clinic — a multi-storey ward block that went insolvent at the end of 2022 and has stood unused since. Because it emptied so recently the interiors are still furnished; hr television found patient and staff files lying open on tables and floors, which is how it got on the map at all.

⚠️ That is also the problem. After the September 2024 broadcast the data-protection officer had police attend and lock the records room, and by January 2025 police were investigating several people for entering illegally. The parent company, Sirius Health Care Holding, is itself under investigation. This is the one site on this map with active, named police interest in people who go inside.
next: Do not walk in. If you want it, it has to come through the insolvency administrator in writing — and the file situation means the answer will probably be no.

name: Altes Bahnbetriebswerk
body:
One of only four places in your whole radius where a pilot has both flown a bando and said where it was. A 2021 freestyle video states it flat in the description — “FPV Flight at the Betriebswerk Heidelberg (Bando)” — which is exactly the disclosure the German scene normally refuses.

An abandoned railway depot: engine sheds, pits, long clear-span volumes. The position is confirmed against OpenStreetMap rather than inferred from the footage.

⚠️ Bahnstadt is one of Germany's largest redevelopment sites and has been building over the old railway land for years. Check it still stands before you drive.
next: Verify existence first — satellite, then a look from the street. If it survived, it is a proven spot rather than a hopeful one.

name: Lore-Bauer-Halle
body:
A municipal hall in Idstein where pilots flew FPV with the owner's permission and published it under the hall's real name in 2018 — two videos, two channels, the same week. The reason it is not hidden is precisely that it was allowed.

That makes this a permission precedent rather than a bando: a named hall, a named town, and evidence the answer was once yes. The owner is the municipality, which is a reachable counterparty.
next: Ask the Stadt Idstein, and cite the 2018 sessions — a documented earlier yes is the strongest opener you have anywhere on this map.

name: Kaserne Babenhausen — the listed core
body:
Correction to this map's own "ruled out" entry. The bulk of the barracks did come down — but 21 listed monument buildings, 12 large residential blocks and 11 halls are still standing and still awaiting renovation, plus a 1955 water tower. The Hessischer VGH struck down the development plan on 21 Jan 2025 and Bonava withdrew, cancelling 530 flats — so the timetable has slipped, not closed.

Why this is the best single lead in the region: the owner has already said yes to almost exactly what you want. The Konversionsgesellschaft ran organised photo walks — 78 photographers across 14 walks, inside some of the buildings. That is a documented precedent, with a named company to ring.
next: Ring the Konversionsgesellschaft Kaserne-Babenhausen and cite the photo walks. If you make one phone call from this entire map, make it this one.

name: ABB / Hitachi Energy works
body:
The largest empty industrial volume anywhere in this radius: roughly 160,000 m² of heavy-electrical multi-bay production halls, in industrial use for over 120 years. The last employees left for good in 2021 and it has been brownfield since.

A logistics developer is turning it into "CTPark Hanau" — but demolition is not scheduled until the end of 2027, which leaves a real window. Multi-bay halls with overhead crane runs are the closest thing in the region to Zone-class interior volume.
next: Two routes: the developer, or Stadt Hanau Stadtentwicklung. A developer holding a site for two years before demolition has little to lose by saying yes.

name: YMOS-Areal
body:
About 63,000 m² of former automotive-supplier plant — pressing shops and chrome-plating halls — on a five-hectare site. The company went insolvent in August 2009 and it has been derelict ever since; local press called a walk across it "a journey through a place of decay".

Contamination is what has kept it standing: a data-centre proposal was still only being discussed in May 2026. That same contamination is the reason nobody will formally let you in.
next: Stadt Obertshausen Stadtplanung. Expect the soil report to be the reason for a no.

name: Bruchseehotel
body:
A purpose-built conference and spa hotel by the lake — about 70 rooms in a multi-storey block. Closed mid-2022, then refugee accommodation, empty since; upkeep was running at roughly €20,000 a month.

The Kreis Bergstraße has published an official sale tender in 2026, with a notary in Heppenheim running the bidding. A building being actively shown to bidders is the easiest permission ask there is — the owner wants people walking through it.
next: Kreis Bergstraße Gebäudewirtschaft, or the notary handling the tender. Ask while the bidding is open.

name: Reha-Klinik Taunus I + II
body:
Two interconnected multi-storey clinic blocks beside the Kurpark — and the freshest vacancy on this entire map. The buildings were emptied on 7 April 2026, and the owner confirmed in January 2026 that it intends to sell.

Freshly emptied means intact: floors, fittings, glazing, no vegetation. It also means the shortest window before a buyer changes everything.
next: Deutsche Rentenversicherung Bund owns it; Stadt Bad Nauheim is the softer first call. Move on this one early.

name: Siesmayer-Karrée
body:
A former psychiatric clinic of eleven brick pavilion buildings from 1891–95, plus kitchen and admin blocks — multi-storey, many windows, set in parkland, partly listed. Empty since 2016; a student-housing conversion was dropped as too costly and the site transfers to the state property agency in 2026.

Eleven separate buildings in a park is structurally the closest thing in Hessen to the Grabowsee layout.
next: The university and the state property agency both hold cards. ⚠️ It sits directly beside an active university hospital with helicopter traffic — that alone may rule out flying regardless of ground permission.

name: Gail-Gelände
body:
Gießen's last big industrial brownfield — roughly 17 hectares of a former steam brickworks and clay-goods factory: large production halls plus a listed Ringofen. Production ended around 1997 and the press calls it an industrial ruin.

The city rejected the owner's housing proposal on 29 July 2026 and wants a technology park instead, so nothing is moving. ⚠️ A few buildings are in use as storage and a gym, and firms keep material in the yard — this is not an empty site.
next: The owner-developer, or Stadt Gießen planning. Note the partial occupation before you assume nobody is watching.

name: Former Sportarena / SportScheck
status: Owned by the city's own developer
body:
A multi-storey retail block of about 5,000 m² on the main shopping street, empty since spring 2024 after the Signa collapse, and bought in January 2025 by the city's own development company. A year later it was still being used only for pop-ups and public debates, with no permanent use decided.

Big open floorplates with column grids — a very different flying problem from a hall, and a rare one.
next: The purest permission route on this map: a municipal company that is openly looking for interim uses. Pitch it as one.

name: Sporthalle Wettinerstraße
body:
A sports hall carrying an explicit abandoned:building=sports_hall tag in OpenStreetMap, with a real street address. A single clear-span indoor volume with a sprung floor is the ideal whoop and 3-inch space, and abandoned ones are vanishingly rare.

⚠️ This came from a mapping database, not from press or a site visit. OSM abandonment tags rot — verify from the street before you invest anything in it.
next: Unverified. Drive past first; if it is genuinely empty, the owner is worth finding.

name: Papierfabrik Ph. Heil Söhne
body:
A paper mill on Pfungstädter Straße carrying disused:man_made=works in OpenStreetMap, with a separate industrial hall building mapped inside it. 6.7 km from your door — by far the closest industrial candidate this search has produced.

⚠️ Treat as unconfirmed. The company's own website was still listed and I could not reach it to check; "disused works" may mean production ceased while the firm trades on, or that the halls stand empty. No press coverage was found either way.
next: Cheap to check — it is a fifteen-minute drive. Look from Pfungstädter Straße before doing anything else. There is a phone number on the OSM record.

name: Ziegelei Nath & Oeder
body:
A Hoffmann ring kiln with a partly collapsed roof, a chimney standing above the treeline, a transformer tower and a loading area with crane remains. Production ended in 1969; abandoned in 2008 for acute structural danger; monument-protected since the 1970s.

Owned by the City of Wiesbaden — the cleanest permission path of anything on this map.

But a 16-year-old fell through that roof in January 2024, so assume it is being secured or reassessed.
next: Ask the city — then confirm it hasn't been sealed since the 2024 fall.

name: Klosterruine Heiligenberg
body:
An early-Romanesque monastery chapel ruin with the remains of a Gothic tower, its choir rebuilt in 1831 using tracery salvaged from Bensheim-Gronau.

Tracery openings and a standing tower stub, thirteen kilometres out — genuinely usable geometry rather than a single wall fragment, and it's a public ruin rather than a fenced site.
next: Check who manages the ruin before flying — monument sites usually want asking.

name: Burg Frankenstein
body:
Tagged open access with no entry fee, and there's real structure here: a gate tower, two towers rebuilt in the 19th century, a chapel of 1474, a battery tower and neck ditches.

Owned by Staatliche Schlösser und Gärten Hessen. Their drone policy could not be confirmed — the relevant page was dead — so assume a state-managed monument wants permission.
next: Ask the state monuments body. Free public access is not the same as flight permission.

name: Burg Lindenfels
body: The best castle geometry in the Odenwald for flying: the main ruin plus the 23 m Bürgerturm standing roughly 200 m away. Two tall separated structures give you actual lines between things, which a single wall stub never does.
next: Town-managed — enquire with the municipality.

name: Kläranlage Waldacker
body:
Mapped explicitly as out of service, with a citation to both a survey and a municipal document — unusually well evidenced for this kind of record. A full municipal basin layout, no fencing recorded, and no airspace problem at this position.

The closest disused sewage works to Darmstadt. Its 2024–26 physical condition is unverified, so treat this as a reconnaissance trip rather than a plan.
next: Drive past and look first, then approach the Gemeinde if it's still standing.

name: Alte Kirche, Klein-Zimmern
body:
A disused church on Kirchplatz, listed as a protected monument. Small but intact, and there is a second candidate nearby: the former monastery church in Dieburg at 49.89827 N, 8.84426 E, roughly the same distance out.

Two disused ecclesiastical buildings within a few kilometres of each other and of the Dieburg model club — worth combining into one trip.
next: Parish or municipality holds the keys. Modest subjects, easy asks.

name: Klosterruine Sankt Wolfgang
body:
A monastery ruin north-east of you, surfaced independently by two separate passes of the data — which is a reasonable signal that it genuinely stands.

Detail beyond its position and status is thin; nobody has documented it in the urbex literature I could reach.
next: Unresearched enough to be worth being the first to look.

name: Church ruin, Hangen-Wahlheim
body: A church ruin west of the Rhine. Read the coordinate, not the name. This sits in Hangen-Wahlheim, a hamlet belonging to Alsheim — and there is a completely separate village called Hangen-Weisheim in the same district. One earlier source conflated them, which would send you to the wrong place entirely.
next: Punch in 49.78070, 8.33556. Do not search the village name.

name: Skilift Tromm
body:
The only genuinely dead ski lift in the Odenwald with documentation behind it. Out of service since 2004, when a lightning strike burned out the valley station and every carrier. A T-bar lift on portal pylons; the first pylon, the valley station remains and the top station all survive and have been photographed.

⚠️ Its coordinates are unverified, and the drag lift that appears in map data at 49.5649, 8.8074 is not this one — that's about 4 km south and still active. Pin position here is approximate.

Every other Odenwald lift I checked is still running, so don't go looking for a second one.
next: Confirm the location from the ropeway archive photos before driving out.

name: Odenwaldklinik
body:
The best pure FPV geometry in the region — interconnected 5–7 storey blocks, stairwells, a roof terrace, an underground thermal spa and pool, a former 197-bed clinic empty since 2013. Satellite confirms a real multi-building complex on a wooded slope.

Correction worth knowing: a fire in the former kitchen on 28 April 2025 — police reported four youths running from the building — is what turned the screw. May 2025 reporting still said there was no security service and no cameras. By that June almost all entrances had been sealed, security was stepped up, and signage went up warning that trespass will not be tolerated. Visitor reports describe police presence through 2025–26.

Add arson in April 2025 and another fire in May 2026, asbestos in the fabric, an insolvent owner and a pending forced auction.

Conflicting reports, stated plainly: one sweep found the entrances sealed and security stepped up from June 2025; a second, working from the same local paper, found no guard and no cameras, with police repeatedly called but never finding anyone. I cannot reconcile those, so treat the security situation as unknown rather than favourable.
next: Effectively burnt out and watched, and it burned again in May 2026. The owner went insolvent, so there is no permission route left, and the town treats entry as a criminal matter. Exterior only.

name: Reha-Klinik Göttmann
body:
Over 100 rooms across 6,300 m² of interior, many interlinked wings plus a park. No patients since 2002, windows boarded against vandalism, confirmed still derelict as of late 2024.

Rambling in exactly the way that suits proximity flying. But it is described as monitored with entry forbidden, it sits in the middle of the village so there's no discretion at all, and the owners are an inheritance community the local paper calls hard to reach.
next: Good geometry, bad odds, no privacy.

name: Kinderkurheim Haus Herne
body:
A 1955 children's convalescent home on a 27,000 m² hillside plot, empty since 1977 and well documented by urbex channels. The village's own website says it stands empty, is privately owned and entry is forbidden.

What lifts it above the other ruins: the owner permitted a concert on the site in September 2024. Of every derelict building here, this is the one where asking has a real chance.
next: Write to the owner citing the 2024 concert as precedent.

name: Klinikum Eberstadt
body:
Architecturally the finest thing in the region: 4.6 hectares holding a listed 1903 ensemble of four symmetrical sandstone buildings with slate roofs and a clock tower, plus a 1975 hospital high-rise. Empty since around 2020, no development progress as of mid-2024.

Then the city wired it up. Since 20 May 2025 the whole site has real-time video surveillance connected to a security service with immediate police notification, plus new fencing and signage. Two people were caught within days and the city pressed charges.

Also note a prison sits in the same district.
next: The one site on this map I'd tell you to simply leave alone.

name: Naturfreundehaus RimDiDim
body:
A burnt-out ruin since arson in 2001 — main building, tower, swimming pool, outbuildings. Described as severely at risk of collapse, and 2025 visitors report much of it has already come down.

The perimeter fence is flattened, but there are documented police patrols and an occasional guard. Owner is an unknown foreign investor.

New: it was a real FPV spot — a local pilot posted two freestyle runs here in June 2021, with a separate aerial video confirming the site. So the verdict below is about its condition in 2025, not about whether anyone ever flew it.
next: Small, genuinely collapsing, and patrolled. Not worth the drive.

name: Lokschuppen (Bw Aschaffenburg)
body:
The last surviving roundhouse of a locomotive depot that opened around 1893 and closed in 1988 — the rest of the site went in 2004 for a ring road. Still standing and decaying as of March 2025, when the local paper asked what happens to it next.

That article is paywalled, so owner and plans are unknown. Urbex photo series show inspection pits, stairs and washrooms intact.

The best unexploited lead here: the urbex map that lists it keeps coordinates behind membership.
next: Read the paywalled March 2025 article — it likely answers ownership outright.

name: August-Euler-Flugplatz
body:
Looks like the obvious open-space option. It is the worst choice on the map.

It is a live special airfield operated by the university — capped at 400 movements a year, but live — so it carries its own 1.5 km zone. And the ground itself is simultaneously a nature reserve, a priority FFH site and part of a bird-protection area, breeding ground-nesting species including wheatear and hoopoe.

Recreational flying over those designations needs the conservation authority's express consent, and in this district a formal exemption from the reserve's own model-aircraft ban on top.
next: Avoid entirely. Same applies to the Griesheimer Düne and Griesheimer Sand.

name: Klinikum Darmstadt helipad
body:
The finding that catches people out. The hospital's helipad is registered as an airfield, so it carries a full 1.5 km zone rather than the 100 m that applies to hospitals generally.

That circle covers Luisenplatz, the Hauptbahnhof, TU Stadtmitte and the Herrngarten. Mathildenhöhe sits about 80 m outside the edge; the Bahnhofsviertel is 0.31 km outside.

Consent here comes from the hospital and airfield side — not from air traffic control, and nothing to do with Frankfurt.
next: Assume the city centre is closed unless you've asked the hospital.

name: Egelsbach airfield
body:
A commercial airfield about 10 km due north with a 1.5 km buffer. Its old control zone was converted to advisory airspace back in 2016, so it has no CTR of its own.

Far enough out to be irrelevant to the city — and worth noting because the widely repeated claim that Darmstadt is “about 3 km from Egelsbach” is simply wrong for the centre.
next: Not a constraint for city flying. Do respect the buffer itself.

name: Muna Münster
body:
The bunkers of a former air-force ammunition depot, later one of NATO's most important special-weapons sites, holding nuclear warheads into 1991.

They physically stand. But roughly 250 hectares remain contaminated with unexploded ordnance and only about 26 have been cleared — at current rates full clearance is estimated in the region of a thousand years. The site is fenced, the municipality has an explicit entry ban, and it doubles as a bison and wild-horse enclosure.

One bunker houses a museum with seasonal opening hours. That's the way in.
next: This is a physical hazard, not a paperwork one. Visit the museum instead.

name: Bettingbergtunnel
body:
The find of this whole search. A 730 m disused railway tunnel, curved, asphalted and open to the public as a cycle route from May to September. Curved means you cannot see the far portal from the entrance, which is exactly what makes a tunnel worth flying.

No FPV footage of it exists anywhere I could find. For a structure this good and this accessible, that is unusual.

It shuts from October to April — that closure is bat protection, not administrative, so it is taken seriously.
next: The binding authority is the Untere Naturschutzbehörde at Landratsamt Main-Spessart, since the bat closure gates any filming. Landholders are Markt Triefenstein and Gemeinde Kreuzwertheim. Fastest reality-check: the ADFC organiser who has led rides through it.

name: Großer Holzmannbogen
body:
A 140 m disused railway tunnel on the old Spessartrampe alignment — lit, 4.3 m wide, and accessible year-round rather than seasonally.

Shorter and straighter than the Bettingbergtunnel, but the year-round access makes it the fallback when the bigger one is shut for bats. Both portals are close together: the far end is at 50.01624 N, 9.34776 E.
next: Same region as the Schwarzkopftunnel site; part of the Kulturweg Spessartrampe. Confirm with the Gemeinde Laufach before flying inside.

name: Klingenberger Dekoramik
body:
The best derelict industrial subject found east of Darmstadt: two chimneys from 1905 and 1911, roller kilns, a press hall and a boiler house. The former Albert-Werke ceramics plant, empty since 2022.

No demolition plan is on record, and no drone footage exists.

The complication is ownership: local press reported in December 2025 that the owner has gone silent — Funkstille — with debts outstanding. A published works-museum phone line probably no longer answers.
next: Go via Stadt Klingenberg am Main. They are publicly frustrated at being unable to reach the owner, so they will know who actually holds the title.

name: Henneburg
body:
Serious castle geometry: two 25 m keeps, two hall ruins and a 150 m underground wall passage. Two tall separated towers give you lines between structures rather than a single stub to orbit.

The towers close from 15 October to 31 March.

Same town as the Klettersteinbruch below, so one trip covers both.
next: Stadtprozelten tourism office handles access: 09392 9847222.

name: Freudenburg
body:
A 32 m keep, town-owned, free to enter, and open year-round — the least gated castle on this list.

Height is what makes it useful: a 32 m tower gives genuine vertical relief in a region that is mostly flat river valley.
next: Town-owned and freely accessible on foot. Ask the Stadt Freudenberg about flying rather than assuming free entry implies it.

name: Burg Wildenberg
body:
The best window and arcade openings of any ruin found — gaps you can actually thread rather than walls to fly around. A Staufer-era castle ruin in the eastern Odenwald.

Privately owned by the Fürsten zu Leiningen, which sounds forbidding but is actually an advantage: there is a single identifiable owner to write to, rather than a municipality or an absent investor.
next: Write to the Leiningen estate administration. One owner, one answer.

name: Schwenk conveyor bridge
body:
A 285 m steel conveyor bridge spanning the Main at the Schwenk cement works, replacing a wartime cable car. Conveyor galleries are prime FPV geometry.

This is a working plant, not a ruin — but organised access is demonstrably granted: a documented works tour ran in June 2023 and the disaster-relief agency held a full exercise inside the works and quarry in 2024.
next: Ring the works on 09353 7970 and ask about a filming visit. They already run tours.

name: Alter Flugplatz Bonames
body:
A US Army helicopter field that closed in 1992 and became a public park. What survives is unusually intact: the control tower (now a café kitchen), a small hangar used for concerts, eleven concrete helipads and the 750 m runway at full length. The fence was torn down.

It also sits just north of the Frankfurt control zone rather than inside it, which is what makes it worth considering at all.

The catch: it is now a nature-education site in the Nidda floodplain, so park and conservation rules will govern flying regardless of the open access.
next: Ask Grünflächenamt Frankfurt. Free public access to a park is not permission to fly in it.

name: Stöffel-Park
body:
The answer to this entire search. A preserved basalt works with the plant left standing — crushers, loading station, boiler and switch house, coal shed, tipper huts, a 1913 forge and an observation tower.

It is the only site found in nine sweeps that publishes a drone policy: €20 per hour plus €7 admission, an Anmeldung Drohnen form at the info desk, and you show your pilot registration. That is a standing industrial plant you can legally fly inside.

Open 1 March to 31 October. Airspace is clear.

One caution: the operator also runs a separate, still-working quarry under the same name nearby. Stay inside the park boundary.
next: Just book it. Nothing else on this map offers permitted flying in real industrial architecture.

name: Grube Georg
body:
The best single structure found anywhere: a 56 m steel headframe sunk in 1952 over a 913 m shaft, with a 70 m gallery deck at 25 m up. Listed as an industrial monument in 1988 and restored with state funds in the mid-nineties.

Standing and rusting, and — unusually — climbable monthly or by arrangement since 2001 through the local citizens' initiative.

I had the geo-zone service queried directly for this point: completely clear.
next: Contact the Bürgerinitiative Willroth or the tourist office of VG Altenkirchen-Flammersfeld, which runs mining tours.

name: Rabenscheider Tunnel
body:
At 1,114 m this is the third-longest rideable former railway tunnel in Germany, and it opened as a public cycle tunnel in August 2022. An oversized oval bore, built 1936–39, which housed a bomb-proof aero-engine plant in 1944–45.

Longer than anything else on this map by a wide margin.

Confirmed bat hibernation closure every winter, with the lighting tuned for bats — so roughly April to October, shared with cyclists.
next: Public access is established; the question is flying, not entry. Ask the Lahn-Dill-Kreis conservation authority.

name: Aartalbahn tunnel group
body:
Four disused tunnels within a few kilometres, 762 m combined, all cut through solid rock with no reported structural damage, on a line that has been a protected monument since 1987.

Laufenseldener 287 m (here) · Hohensteiner 169 m at 50.19507, 8.05683, which bores through the rock the castle stands on and has castle-style corbelled portal towers · Michelbacher 156 m, a curved bore, at 50.22153, 8.03634 · Adolfsecker 150 m at 50.16008, 8.07719.

Time-sensitive: Hessen approved €45 m in 2026 partly to reactivate this line. The window may be closing.
next: The Arbeitskreis Aartalbahn runs draisine tours and is shifting onto exactly this segment — the people to ask. Assume bat roosts and avoid November to March.

name: Nistertal Viadukt
body:
Eleven arches, roughly 300 m long and 40 m high — at the time of building the largest tamped-concrete structure in Germany. The trackbed became a cycle and walking route in 2014 and the entry ban was formally lifted.

The one caveat that genuinely bites: it sits inside a bird-protection area plus an FFH site. Of all the nature designations, a Vogelschutzgebiet is the one that matters most.
next: Check breeding season with the Untere Naturschutzbehörde before anything else.

name: Hotel Eden Parc
body:
The one genuine grand-spa ruin in the region: built 1929–31 by Wilhelm Kreis as the state Kurhotel, a protected monument, about 5,900 m² with 36 rooms plus a separate 4,400 m² wing.

Empty since 2018 and described as structurally sound but needing extensive modernisation — derelict rather than collapsing, which is the good kind.

A forced auction was set for 8 July 2026 at €4.31 m appraised value. The outcome is unknown — and it decides whether this becomes approachable or sealed.

No urbex coverage found, which cuts both ways.
next: Find out who bought it. The Amtsgericht record will name the new owner; then ask for a film permit. No legal access exists today.

name: Burg Grenzau
body:
A 32 m four-storey keep — the only triangular one in Germany. A three-sided tower gives you edges and changing faces to work rather than a plain cylinder.

Inside an FFH area covering the Brexbach and Saynbach valleys.
next: Worth pairing with Grube Georg and the Stöffel-Park — all three sit within about 25 km of each other.

name: Schloss Schaumburg
body:
A 42 m tower — the tallest structure on this map — on a three-wing neo-Gothic palace with octagonal basalt corner turrets, above the Lahn.

It runs a café, museum, concerts and exhibitions, so there is an organisation to approach rather than an absent owner. Held by an investor group since 2012, with the gatehouses restored by 2018.

No protection overlay.
next: It hosts public events, so a filming request has an obvious route in.

name: Burg Ardeck
body:
A 21 m five-storey keep only about 5 m in diameter — a genuinely slender free-standing shaft, which is rare and makes for a very different flying subject than a fat cylinder.

Described in the record as freely accessible, with no internal stair. No nature or airspace overlay at all — one of the cleanest points on this map.
next: Free-standing, freely accessible, unrestricted. Verify on the ground, then fly.

name: Burg Königstein
body:
One of Germany's largest castle ruins, with the keep and most cellars accessible and the vaults rentable for events. Open year-round.

What makes it notable here is administrative rather than architectural: it is owned outright by the town, has a summer events programme, and carries no nature or airspace overlay whatsoever — the cleanest legal picture of any castle found.

Close in, too, at under 40 km.
next: Stadt Königstein already rents the vaults out. Ask them about filming.

name: Adolph-Schacht
body:
A four-storey rectangular rubble-stone shaft tower with a saddle roof, completed 1873, standing as a ruin in the Pitschbachtal. A rubble-stone chimney with a brick crown from around 1850 stands about 250 m away at 50.35188, 7.73215.

An earlier report gave the tower as 25 m; that figure could not be verified, so treat the height as unknown.

Geo-zone clear for both. Ownership and fencing unverified.
next: Recce first — nobody has documented its condition or whether it is fenced.

name: Kirchhofsmühle
body:
Modest in size but unusually well documented: the state monument register itself records it as shut down since 1926 and describes it today as a Bauruine — a building ruin.

That makes it the most officially-confirmed standing ruin on the Lahn, in a region where most of the industrial stock turned out to be demolished. On the Lahn long-distance path, with a mill weir.

Inside the FFH area covering the Lahn valley and its slopes.
next: Small, but a confirmed ruin with a named owner route through Stadt Weilburg.

name: Grube Fortuna
body:
An intact mine surface: winding house with its original 1958 machine, the 1907/08 engine house with water tower, ore bunker, tipping hall and a surviving cable-car pylon. Plus a field-railway museum with fifty-odd locomotives on 2.5 km of 600 mm track.

Run as an active museum with around 20,000 visitors a year, so this is a permission request rather than a free flight — but an organisation that already handles visitors is far easier to ask than an absent landlord.
next: Approach Geowelt Fortuna e.V. — they are a visitor operation and used to requests.

name: Altes Polizeipräsidium — photo tours
body:
The only active, permitted urbex photo-tour operator found in the whole radius. The building belongs to the state of Hessen and is under interim management, and the tours run through that partnership — so the permission is real, not improvised.

The relevant format is the photography one, Fotografieren wo sonst keiner hinkommt, with dates through the autumn. The same operator also runs the Sachsenhausen oil factory, the Fischergewölbe and the old ropeworks.

Drones are not mentioned either way in the conditions — which is negotiating room, not permission.
next: Book a photo tour, meet the guide, then ask about a drone. A tour operator with existing access is the cheapest route to a permitted flight.

name: MFG Weilmünster
body:
Flagged in the community as an exception among model clubs for actually taking on drone and FPV pilots. The club is demonstrably alive — its site was publishing wind readings from the field this week.

Regional television covered FPV racing here in May 2026, following a local 25-year-old pilot heading to the world championship in China. That is a real FPV scene, not a tolerated minority.

An open flying day runs 22 August 2026; whether guests may fly is not stated.
next: The most FPV-friendly club found in any direction. Email the committee before the 22 August event.

name: Verladeturm Im Ohl
body:
The one multi-storey crusher and loading tower that survives anywhere in this direction. Built for the Rousselsche Basaltwerke, it housed the crushing plant and served as the rail loading station. Basalt was worked here from 1880 to 1930, and the town's own account says the works has been left to decay ever since.

A listed monument, and footage of it exists.

Two serious problems. It is fenced and genuinely structurally rotten — walkers report tonne-weight pieces having fallen off, and warn it is not a playground. And it stands directly beside the A 66 and the Frankfurt–Fulda main line, which triggers the 100 m road and rail buffer.
next: The binding constraint here is the road/rail buffer, not conservation law. That is a permission question with conditional routes, so settle it before travelling.

name: Steinbruch Michelnau
body:
A red-basalt quarry with real machinery still standing: a derrick crane with a 20.5 m jib, built 1952 and fully rebuilt in 2012, plus a working winch house and machine hall.

What lifts it above everything else in this direction is the trajectory — Stadt Nidda is actively developing the site as an industrial monument for visitors, so there is a municipal owner with a public-access agenda and a published phone number rather than an absent landlord.

Confirmed clear of nature designations at the point itself. It already appears on the state broadcaster's list of legal lost places, with the interior open during opening hours and tours, and cameras on site.
next: Ring Stadt Nidda on 06043 3173. A town that is building visitor access is the easiest yes on this map after the Stöffel-Park.

name: Kümmelbacher Hof
body:
On architecture alone, the best freestyle object in the entire search. A castle-like estate from around 1800 with a hexagonal four-storey residential tower under a pointed roof, a brewery and malthouse of 1879, a 1920s spa-hotel extension, and two wings each roughly 45–60 m long — with modern glass-and-steel upper floors dropped on top in the early 1960s.

Unused since 2006. A fire in February 2013 opened up the upper floors, so the roof and ceiling voids are already broken through.

A hexagonal tower, two long wings, stacked glass-steel storeys and fire-opened upper floors is an unusually rich combination.

The owner is Pro Seniore, holding it as a strategic reserve and still weighing a reactivation as a retirement village. No demolition pressure.
next: A named, writable company with no deadline is the best lever you get on a ruin this good. Write to Pro Seniore.

name: Kopp-Fabrik
body:
The top find of the Pfalz sweep, and the largest empty floorplate anywhere on this map: five wings, three storeys, about 9,500 m², with daylight from both sides of every wing — which is what makes a factory flyable rather than a dark box.

A shoe factory from the industry whose collapse emptied Pirmasens. Long-term vacancy is documented rather than assumed.
next: Pirmasens is the one town in the region where several derelict factories have named, reachable owners — a foundation, an agent, the city planning office. Start with the city.

name: Palatia-Schuhfabrik
body:
The only site in the Pfalz with a demonstrably art-friendly owner — someone who has already opened the building to creative use rather than merely tolerating it.

Now or never: conversion work is beginning. Once that starts, the empty volume goes.
next: Highest-probability yes in the Pfalz, and the shortest deadline. Ask this month.

name: Binshof
body:
A hotel and spa complex, empty since the end of 2023 after the operator left following 22 years. Rooms are reportedly still furnished — much of it still looks like a working hotel.

Owned by a closed property fund. A sale is described as imminent, which sets the timing: approach the new owner once it completes, before refurbishment begins.

⚠️ Correction since I first staged this: the airfield is not the problem — it is about 6 km away, comfortably outside the 1.5 km buffer. The problem is that the site lies inside an EU bird-protection area in the Rhine floodplain. That is a Natura 2000 designation, so recreational flying there needs the conservation authority's consent outright.
next: Two permissions needed, not one: the new owner and the conservation authority. That makes it a long game.

name: Freizeitbad TAURIS
body:
The best legal-access odds of anything in the whole sweep. A leisure pool standing empty and complete: 25 m hall pool, a 63 m tube slide, flow channel, climbing wall and net, sauna landscape and two outdoor basins. Closed for good in June 2023.

Two facts make it unusually approachable. The owner is the town itself, which has had it on the market for one euro since December 2024. And the regional paper was allowed inside to film the empty building — so a precedent for exactly your request already exists, with the mayor and the operations manager named.

Demolition is also under discussion. The window is open, not indefinite.
next: Cite the newspaper's filming visit as precedent and ask the Stadtbürgermeister. Nothing else on this map has a clearer route in.

name: Hallenbad Münster
body:
The closest disused pool to you by a wide margin. Demolition has been recommended since January 2022 and an investor surfaced in November 2024, but mapping data still showed the building standing at the end of 2024.

Status genuinely uncertain — this is the one site on the map I would ring about before starting the car.
next: Phone the municipality first. Fifteen kilometres is a short trip, but not to look at a car park.

name: Viktoriastift
body:
The most interesting interior of the entire search. A three-wing neo-baroque estate of 1919–22 in sandstone ashlar: a manor with a hexagonal roof turret and a double-height reception hall panelled in oak with stucco and a mock fireplace, coffered ceilings above — plus a large barn with driveable high threshing floors and an administration building with big stables.

Empty since 1971, yet not a collapsing ruin: it has been a protected monument since 1990 and the roofs were renewed in 1995, 2003 and 2005. Fifty-five years vacant and still structurally sound is rare.

A holiday-park conversion is planned; what happens to the historic buildings is not stated anywhere.
next: The project developer is named and reachable in Frankfurt. Ask before the conversion decides the buildings' fate.

name: Kurmittelhaus
body:
Architecturally the loveliest thing found: a 1911 Jugendstil bath house mixing half-timber and baroque forms under an elaborate roofscape, with a fountain hall carrying an Art Deco glass mosaic in blues and greens flecked with gold, three mineral springs, and underground areas with glass cylinders.

Bathing stopped in 2014 and it has been unused since. Protected, and needing eight figures of restoration.

It is a single grand hall rather than a course — but the owner is the city of Bad Kreuznach, which even staged an exhibition of seventy student proposals for its future. A public owner with documented openness is the most promising permission request on this map.
next: Ask the city. They have already invited outside ideas about this building once.

name: Thingstätte Heidelberg
body:
A vast Nazi-era open-air amphitheatre on the Heiligenberg — 56 tiers of seating and two towers, cut into the hillside — and freely accessible by day.

The tiered bowl gives you something almost nothing else here does: a large, open, symmetrical form with hard edges to trace and no roof to trap you.

Given what it was built for, treat it with some care about how footage is framed.
next: Publicly accessible, so the question is city drone rules rather than entry. Check with Heidelberg.

name: Eistalviadukt
body: A 271 m viaduct standing 35 m high, disused since 1988. Height and span together make a viaduct one of the better freestyle structures — you get arches to thread and a long line to run.
next: Establish the owner — disused rail structures usually sit with the infrastructure company or the municipality.

name: AQUAtoll
body:
A 1990 leisure pool with a distinctive glass dome, several indoor and outdoor basins, a wild-water channel and slides. Closed in 2022.

The town is transferring it to an investor for a symbolic sum with reopening planned for 2028, and geothermal test drilling was already under way in 2025 — so the investor, not the city, is who to ask.

Worth citing in any request: the site featured as a Lost Place in an exhibition at the Haus der Geschichte in Stuttgart.
next: Approach the investor rather than the municipality, and do it before the 2028 rebuild starts.

name: Wasserturm Groß-Gerau
body:
The find of the Ried, and it is close: a 45 m water tower of 1928/29 holding a 500 m³ tank.

Decommissioned in autumn 2022 — the tank was drained, use of the upper floors ended, and the viewing platform closed to the public on 1 September 2022 after a survey found structural problems with an intermediate floor.

That combination is unusual and useful: a tall, slender, recently-emptied municipal structure with no water in it, no public visitors to endanger, and no redevelopment announced. It is not a ruin — which means there is a functioning owner to ask rather than an absent one.
next: Ask the town or its utility. A structure they have just closed and not yet decided about is the easiest kind of yes to get.

name: Coreum
body:
I listed this earlier as a rentable hall without registering that it sits in exactly the area you are asking about, eighteen kilometres away.

It is a construction-machinery centre with 120,000 m² of outdoor terrain laid out as fifteen themed worlds, hundreds of machines and vehicles across it, plus halls, a hotel and conference space. It rents itself out as an event location for groups from 2 to 850 with technical support.

Earthworks, machinery, gantries and made ground over twelve hectares is a far better freestyle proposition than a mown club field — and it is a business whose job is to say yes to bookings.
next: Ring their event side and ask about a filming slot. Of everything within 20 km, this is the most likely permitted flight.

name: Kläranlage Biebesheim
body:
A sewage works mapped explicitly as außer Betrieb — out of service — on industrial land in the Rhine plain. The same kind of subject as the disused works at Rödermark: circular and rectangular basins, walkways, plant housing.

Condition in 2026 is unverified; this is a reconnaissance trip, not a plan.
next: Drive past and look, then approach the Gemeinde if it is still standing.

name: Generator- und Pumpenhaus
body:
A ruined building from around 1900 that belonged to the Hohenaue estate. It housed a steam engine and an electricity generator driving a pump, used to keep the fields clear of water when the Rhine flooded.

Small — a single structure, not a course — but it is a genuine, mapped ruin with a documented history, five minutes from the Trebur model field where FPV is permitted in writing.
next: Worth combining with a Trebur session rather than a trip of its own.

name: Kühkopf-Knoblochsaue
body:
The reason the Ried looks emptier than it should. Hessen's largest nature reserve, 2,440 hectares, protected since 1952 and a Natura 2000 site, filling the whole Rhine loop west of Riedstadt.

Recreational flying over a nature reserve or a Natura 2000 area needs the conservation authority's express consent — the self-executing exemption in the regulation excludes sport and leisure, so it does not help you.

This single designation rules out most of the attractive open river landscape between Riedstadt, Stockstadt and Erfelden.
next: Treat the whole Rhine loop as closed unless you have written consent. Everything else in the Ried sits outside it.

name: Ausbesserungswerk
body: An old railway works with big halls, rated beginner-friendly — and the closest bando in this database to Darmstadt, about 55 km south.
next: Open.

name: Ziegelei Hockenheim
body: A large brickworks with many big open halls. Around 60 km from Darmstadt.
next: Open.

name: Bismarckturm
body: A tower spot — vertical structure rather than interior.
next: Open.

name: Klinik Neukirchen
body: A huge hospital campus with housing blocks and a swimming hall — the closest thing to a Zone-class complex in Hessen, about 130 km north of Darmstadt. Noted as set back in woodland and well screened from the road.
next: Open, and unusually discreet.

name: Bad Wildbad
body: A Black Forest spot on the community list.
next: Open.

name: Dasenstein
body: A vineyard crag in the Black Forest.
next: Open.

name: Völklinger Hütte
body: UNESCO ironworks. Another site whose fame does not translate — zero FPV evidence was found anywhere.
next: Aerial footage requires written permission.

name: Saarschleife
body: The Saar loop and its treetop walk — a landscape spot, and the only Saarland entry on the list.
next: Open.

name: Dronula 1 Indoor Arena
body: A 1,500 m² permanent indoor drone-racing track, reported as the first of its kind in Germany.
next: Commercial and bookable.

name: Silag-Gelände · ehem. Seidenweberei Niepmann
body: The site behind The Zone. Independently confirmed by the community database, which lists it anonymously as “Fabrik” on Wuppertaler Straße: smaller halls, rooms and corridors, open windows, good rear courtyards. Difficulty rated medium.
next: Freely enterable. Note the sim connection is my inference — no public source states it.

name: Gießerei Hagen
body: Narrow corridors and small windows. Advanced.
next: Open.

name: ThyssenKrupp Testturm
body: The 246 m elevator test tower. Listed on a community map under a “permission granted” layer — one of only three such entries.
next: Listed as permission-based.

name: Verlassenes Parkhaus
body: A large multi-storey car park standing empty. Open decks and ramps — a very different flying problem from a hall.
next: Open.

name: Wasserhäusle
body: A small structure spot on the Danube.
next: Open.

name: Whoop Wald
body: A woodland whoop spot rather than a bando — trees, gaps, natural gates.
next: Open.

name: Fabrik Ratingen
body: Tight and compact — for experienced pilots.
next: Open.

name: Altes Schmelzwerk
body: The database links 2024 freestyle footage here. Plausibly the site behind the well-known “Bando No. 2 Lostplace Hamm” video, though that is not confirmed.
next: Open.

name: Zeche Zollverein
body: UNESCO coking and coal complex — headframes, coking halls, conveyor bridges. Famous in the scene partly because of the tension: pilots have organised meetups here, and one video description thanks another pilot for arranging the rendezvous.
next: Grounds walkable, but private, artistic, racing and practice drone flight are banned across the whole outdoor site. Editorial only, in writing.

name: Zementwerk Ennigerloh
body: Tight gaps, remote. Rated advanced.
next: Open.

name: Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord
body: The former Thyssen blast-furnace works, now a public park — furnaces, gas holders, ore bunkers, walkways at every level. The community note is candid: a huge bando, but heavily visited, so fly by the rules and use small quads to avoid trouble.
next: Freely enterable as a park, but drones are prohibited for private pilots. Commercial only via the city.

name: Ziemestalbrücke
body: An 1895 lattice viaduct on a disused line in Thuringia — a classic structure spot rather than a bando. On the spot list plus two dedicated forum threads.
next: Freely walkable.

name: Zeche Niederberg
body: Two preserved headframes and a machine house. A forum flight report exists, but pilots are turned away by site workers about half the time.
next: Fencing contested; roughly even odds.

name: Ehemaliges Ferienheim
body: Very tight — the database explicitly warns it is not for beginners.
next: Open.

name: Eisenwerk Zwickau
body: Described as a huge bando with open access — many buildings and large open halls.
next: Open access per the database.

name: Bando a. d. Mauritiusbrauerei
body: Small and beginner-friendly.
next: Open.

name: Dreiländereck
body: Tight rooms plus one larger hall.
next: Open.

name: FPV München
body: The Munich scene's listed flying spot.
next: Open.

name: Ausweichparkplatz
body: An overflow car park used as a practice spot near Munich.
next: Open.

name: Fabrik Güsten
body: Small, but the tower can be dived from outside.
next: Open.

name: Ehem. Bahnbetriebswerk Wahren
body: Halls plus two roomy towers. An active railway depot sits next door, so expect company.
next: Derelict; neighbouring depot in use.

name: Bando am Bayerischen Bahnhof
body: A tinywhoop spot — small windows, columns and corridors rather than big volumes.
next: Small copters only, realistically.

name: Reichsbahn-Ausbesserungswerk
body: Open halls, windows and corridors. Rated beginner-friendly.
next: Open.

name: Alte Spitzenfabrik
body: The find of this sweep. The only site anywhere in Germany where the database records that the owners know FPV pilots and are completely fine with it. Open meadow, a rear garden for small copters, two bridges.
next: Welcomed. If one place deserves a message before you drive, it is this one.

name: Ehem. Magnesitwerk
body: Huge, with tall halls and a lot of variety — one of the larger entries in the database.
next: Open.

name: Ehem. Wasserkraftwerk Canitz
body: An all-rounder; the interior suits 2–3.5 inch quads.
next: Open.

name: funpark · Kraftwerk Meppen-Hüntel
body: A decommissioned 1974 gas power station over 60 hectares, with a 131 m cooling tower. Home of Europe's largest FPV freestyle festival, running since at least 2019 — and the organiser also runs the community spot map.
next: Ticketed, on event dates only. The one unambiguously permitted freestyle destination in the country.

name: Ferropolis
body: The “city of iron” — giant bucket-wheel excavators on a peninsula. Visually the most spectacular industrial site in Germany.
next: Drones expressly forbidden for private individuals on safety grounds, with legal action threatened.

name: Luftmunitionslager
body: Grass floor and hidden away — the database's recommended bando for a first attempt.
next: Open.

name: Erlebnisbad Basso
body: An abandoned 1993 leisure pool, sealed since 2009: waterslide shell, wave pool, flooded cellar. The database entry says flatly that it is known from countless YouTube videos — many open windows, tight corridors, open halls.
next: Freely enterable. Noted as screened from view, with parking right at the spot.

name: Altes Möbelhaus
body: A relatively well-known lost place — but the database warns that getting in is not guaranteed.
next: Access uncertain.

name: Beelitz-Heilstätten
body: The famous sanatorium complex. Included because everyone asks — but despite its fame, no FPV freestyle footage could be found, only camera-drone material from outside.
next: Fenced to 2 m with private security; trespassers reported to police.

name: “Hamburg Bando”
body: Listed with an address on Neuländer Straße and described only as “a factory”. The likely — not certain — match is the old New-York Hamburger Gummi-Waaren rubber works, roughly 200 m long and three storeys.
next: Under redevelopment pressure; may not survive.

name: Teufelsberg
body: The Cold-War listening station on a rubble hill — radomes, towers, graffiti. Documented freestyle sessions and cinematic FPV both exist.
next: Ticketed, roughly €12, open daily until sunset. Flying is on the operator's terms.

name: Verlassener Sowjet-Flughafen
body: A big metal hall, outlying buildings, bunkers and open field. The database notes never having had trouble with passers-by.
next: Open.

name: Zementfabrik Alsen · “Itzehoe Bando”
body: Once Europe's largest cement works, shut in 1982. Four buildings survive plus a 70 m chimney and a 32 m-diameter concrete mixing tank. An arts association is active on the site.
next: Not fenced, publicly accessible.

name: Heilstätte Grabowsee
body: The closest thing to a Zone-class complex found anywhere in this search. I went through the photographer's 22 photos of it: corridors that run straight for the whole length of a wing with door openings receding one after another, an attic passage lit by windows on both sides under bare roof trusses, rooms with full window grids facing daylight, an assembly hall with a proscenium stage, and half a dozen separate three-storey buildings standing in woodland with open ground between them. Gutted but structurally whole — floors intact, no visible collapse. A 1896 Red Cross tuberculosis sanatorium, then a Soviet military hospital until 1992. And the access is far better than a lost place has any right to be: €10 at the gate, listed with opening hours, 4.7 stars from 725 reviews. Visitors describe ringing the leaseholder to book a slot, getting a short introduction and a site map at the door, and then being left to roam the grounds alone and photograph freely — one calls the buildings “in recht gutem Zustand”. Fifty-nine reviews use the words “lost place”. The one gap is FPV specifically: no footage of it exists and no drone policy is published, so that is the single question left to ask.
next: €10, opening hours listed (Thu from 12:00) but reviewers book other days by phoning the leaseholder on 0175 2425275. Photography is explicitly fine; drones are not mentioned either way, so ask before you drive — do not assume the photo permission covers a quad.

name: Chemiewerk Rüdersdorf
body: The best-known bando in Germany, and the forum evidence says so outright — pilots are told they will reliably meet other FPV flyers there. Hangar-scale halls, concrete silos and conveyor structures. A second pin sits next door at the Betonsteinwerk (52.48849, 13.79591), conveyors only.
next: Freely enterable.

name: Kraftwerk Vogelsang
body: An unfinished Nazi-era power station on the Oder, the only survivor of its type. The database calls it a known bando with two perfect wide-diameter towers for dives, very open, few corridors. Listed on both spot databases.
next: Open. Sits in a nature reserve — a 1998 demolition was stopped by protected species.

name: Oder Bando
body: A proper bando beside the river with a quarry nearby. ⚠️ The published pin lands on a water-police station, which looks like a deliberate decoy — treat the position as approximate.
next: Position unreliable.

name: Zanders / Papierpark
status: 36 ha, and they let people in
body:
A former fine-paper works of about 36 hectares, production ended April 2021. Roughly a dozen substantial structures survive — a 1904 administration block, a 1931 power house by Dominikus Böhm, a 1911 warehouse, bleachery, paper-machine halls, sorting and calendering halls. Several are heritage-listed and the halls were formally inventoried in May 2026, so the fabric is documented and intact rather than gutted.

The best access route in NRW. The city's development company runs guided tours every Monday 16:00–17:30, and has repeatedly opened halls to outsiders: a carnival society, a Christmas market inside the Zentralwerkstatt, a music video shoot, a photo production, an artist working in a hall. No FPV precedent — but a documented film-and-photo precedent, which is closer than anywhere else on this map.

⚠️ It is also an active conversion site; expect fenced construction zones beside the intact halls.
next: Zanders-Entwicklungsgesellschaft (a City of Bergisch Gladbach vehicle), info@zanders.de. Ask as a filming request and cite the shoots they have already hosted.

name: Altes Stadtbad
body:
Disused municipal swimming baths in Jugendstil, pool halls and galleries intact. The city has programmed it since 2024 and it is busier in 2026 than at any point since closure — a youth party, a summer culture season, a Heimatwerkstatt, entomological collections in the side rooms, and a July 2026 installation letting visitors walk across the water.

A pool hall is a rare FPV volume: one clear span, hard surfaces, a gallery to thread.
next: Stadt Krefeld, Fachbereich Kultur — they run the programme and issue the permissions. Pitch it against one of their own event days. ⚠️ Düsseldorf CTR is close; check the boundary.

name: Waldkrankenhaus (Auguste-Viktoria-Stiftung)
body:
One of Germany's first TB sanatoria, built 1900–02, about 6,000 m², heritage-listed. Empty since the last patients left in April 2002 — twenty-four years, which for a listed sanatorium means long corridors, ward wings and stairwells largely as they were left.

The fabric is good enough that it served as a filming location for Babylon Berlin. Broken into in March 2026 by teenagers who were caught via their own footage.
next: Kliniken der Stadt Köln own it and are publicly hunting a buyer at a nominal price — reported repeatedly as "für einen Euro". An owner who wants rid of a building takes calls.

name: St. Barbara-Hospital
body:
A 1905 hospital, 262 beds at peak, on a 42,000 m² site, closed 2013. The roof structure was destroyed by arson in 2021 and there was a second fire in 2024; a man died in a fall inside in 2023.

⚠️ The city has issued a formal Betretungsverbot and the site is hoarded with fines for entry. Ownership is genuinely unsettled — a forced auction ran in February 2026, with one outlet reporting a sale to Luxembourg investors and another reporting the court refusing the Zuschlag.
next: None usable until ownership resolves. Local media call it a Lost Place, which means it is watched.

name: Kabel Premium Pulp & Paper
status: 38 ha mill, developer just bought it
body:
A paper mill that shut in June 2025 after 129 years — about 380,000 m² with full mill halls, machine houses and stock buildings. Sold in October 2025 to a Belgian logistics developer.

⚠️ Short window. January 2026 reporting is headlined “Gelände soll nicht lange brachliegen”, and the buyer builds new-build warehouses, so demolition of the mill fabric is the likely direction.
next: The developer, or Hagen Wirtschaftsförderung which has been publicly involved in the reuse debate.

name: St. Hubertus-Stift
body:
An 87-bed hospital in service since 1895, closed permanently at the end of January 2025 after a failed restructuring. Recent enough that it should still be sealed and undamaged rather than stripped — no fire or vandalism reporting found.

Bought out of the insolvency estate in May 2026 by a local farmer and entrepreneur planning medical practices, a pharmacy and housing. A single named individual is the easiest permission conversation on this list. One secondary source mentions demolition, so move early.
next: The new owner directly. Recent, private, and reachable.

name: St. Josef-Krankenhaus
body:
A regional hospital of 217 beds across three departments, closed at the end of 2022. The developer has said it intends to keep roughly half the building substance, so ward wings and corridors survive rather than being flattened.

The development plan is not expected before 2027, which leaves a planning gap — but Hamm council received a deconstruction timetable in June 2026, so partial demolition may start sooner. Verify before travelling.
next: The developer, or Stadt Hamm planning. No urbex coverage exists, so interior condition is unverified.

name: Klinik Aprath
body:
A former children's TB sanatorium — main building 1910, ward, school and isolation blocks added in the 1920s and 30s — closed at the end of 2006. Twenty years empty, boarded, fenced and under surveillance after vandalism and arson.

⚠️ Two warnings. A demolition permit granted in 2012 was never executed and no reliable current owner could be identified. And the site carries heavy ethical baggage — unethical drug trials on children, with an active witness-research project — so an approach framed as recreational filming will land badly.
next: None identified. Condition evidence is thin: the newest physical confirmation is a 2024 memorial visit, and the detailed survey dates from 2019.

name: Hallenbad Eickel
body:
A municipal indoor pool standing empty, with wall mosaics the city has declined to preserve. The pool hall was still intact as of July 2026, when a city document recorded tree clearance in preparation for demolition. A citizens' initiative is still contesting it.

⚠️ Use it or lose it. Excavators could arrive any week.
next: Stadt Herne owns it, has decided to demolish, and rejected preserving even the mosaics. A request is unlikely to succeed.

name: Vallourec-Areal
body:
The historic 1899 Mannesmann seamless-tube works — two hot-rolling mills on about 900,000 m². Machinery was stripped by January 2024; a newspaper got inside in May 2025 and called it “die verbotene Stadt”, which tells you the scale of the surviving halls.

⚠️ Demolition started in June 2026. Only the heritage-listed buildings are safe bets now — the city has committed to preserving those.
next: The Czech developer holding 83 ha, or the City of Düsseldorf. Escorted access is demonstrably obtainable: a newspaper got a guided visit.

name: Kraftwerk Frimmersdorf
body:
The most spectacular interior volume in NRW — combined machine halls running roughly 650 metres, on a site 1.5 km by 450 m. The last blocks shut in September 2021.

⚠️ And out of reach. The operator is converting the machine house itself into 110,000 m² of office and lab space by 2029, so it is a fenced, contractor-occupied construction site with security. Cooling towers are being blasted progressively. Operational power-station ground: overflight needs the operator's consent.
next: Only a formal media request to the operator, which is unlikely to be granted.

name: Kraftwerk Niederaußem, Blocks A–G
body:
Blocks A through F are all decommissioned — the last pair in March 2024 after reserve duty — leaving the old boiler and turbine houses idle for about two years with no demolition reported.

⚠️ Block K still generates on the same site, so the perimeter is live and secured throughout. No redevelopment project has been named, which means there is no developer to approach.
next: The plant operator only. Realistically closed.

name: Kraftwerk Neurath, Blocks A–E
status: Five blocks idle, two still run
body:
Blocks A through E were shut between 2021 and March 2024; F and G run until 2030. No demolition timeline has been published for the idle blocks.

⚠️ Live generation next door, and the site sits on the edge of the Garzweiler opencast mine — so mine-safety restrictions apply on top of the aviation ones.
next: The plant operator, under the lignite-exit agreement. Not a realistic ask.

name: Kraftwerk Westfalen, Block E
body:
Block E ran only from 2014 to July 2021 and has been idle since. A neighbouring block was cancelled before completion — verify whether a shell exists at all before counting on it.

⚠️ A large battery-storage installation on the same site is being expanded through 2028, so expect construction traffic and an active perimeter.
next: The plant operator. Low priority.

name: Kraftwerk Duisburg-Walsum, Block 9
body:
Block 9 was shut in July 2021 under the coal phase-out with no demolition confirmed. ⚠️ Block 10 operates immediately alongside at 725 MW, which means full perimeter security across the whole complex.

Position is approximate — the block is not separately geocoded, so this pin marks the site rather than the building. Lowest-confidence entry in this region.
next: The plant operator. Listed for completeness rather than opportunity.

name: Mansergh Barracks
status: Sale frozen, may return to military
body:
A large former British Forces barracks, empty since the 2019/20 handover, with accommodation blocks, workshops and stores. The town ran a competition and a masterplan won in 2020.

⚠️ The route closed in October 2025 when the federal government suspended barracks sales nationwide. March 2026: “Alle Pläne liegen auf Eis”. And a June 2026 report says the Bundeswehr continues to assess the site after a British exercise there — it may return to military use. Stay away.
next: None. The federal property agency cannot sell and cannot grant access.

name: Kurhaus Sand
body:
A second Waldlust, and this one is easier. An 1850 grand hotel, listed, closed since about 2006 — and unusually undamaged: the Jagdzimmer is near-original, the dining hall and many guest rooms survive, and the operator reports comparatively little vandalism. A multi-storey hotel block with corridor runs and a large Speisesaal, so there is real interior volume.

The route is the best on this map: a non-profit sells access at €15 per hour. A preservation association and the town's economic development office also run guided tours. Booking a paid hour is a realistic way to reach a filming permission.

⚠️ The Schwarzwaldhochstraße abuts the Nationalpark Schwarzwald — check the boundary before any outdoor line. The interior is the point anyway.
next: Book an hour through the operating gGmbH. Paying for a slot puts you in the building legally, which is the hard part solved.

name: Blautal-Center
body:
A 37,000 m² shopping centre from 1997, one of the largest in the south. Trading ceased in 2024 and it is now a covered ghost town with a handful of tenants left. Multi-level atrium, escalator voids and very long mall corridors — outstanding FPV geometry of a type almost never available.

⚠️ Urgent. Excavators for the successor quarter were scheduled for autumn 2026. That is now.
next: The redevelopment investor, via Stadt Ulm Stadtplanungsamt. Pre-demolition is often the easiest moment to get a yes — nobody is protecting resale value any more.

name: Schwarzwaldklinik (Rehazentrum)
status: Empty 14 years, flown from the air
body:
A former spa clinic on a 75,000 m² site with three mineral springs, empty since a second insolvency in 2011. A large multi-wing complex — one explorer's video is titled “Die Monsteraula”, so there is a big hall volume alongside the ward corridors.

The only Baden-Württemberg site with any drone evidence: aerial footage exists and is named, plus interior walkthroughs from 2025 and 2026. Aerial rather than freestyle — but it proves the site is enterable and being flown.

⚠️ Condition is poor. Small trees now grow on the roof and there was a fire in March 2026, so treat structural integrity as uncertain.
next: Weak. A Chinese investor bought it in 2015 and abandoned plans in 2017; no active owner contact surfaced. Try the Gemeinde Bauamt. Position approximate.

name: Unterirdisches Notkrankenhaus
body:
A purpose-built Cold War casualty clinic that was never used. Not a hall building — its value is long unbroken corridors and connected chambers, which is excellent gate-and-line flying and completely weather-independent. Preserved rather than ruined.

Unauthorised entry is illegal, but the press states guided tours can be arranged, which makes this one of the few permission-realistic sites anywhere.
next: Enquire with Stadt Rottenburg about a tour. The surface address is a school; the facility is beneath it, so the pin is approximate.

name: Alte Schererfabrik
body:
